turns.response_html:
You are pointing out a really exhausting trend in both how we talk about history and how we consume media: the weaponization of cynicism.

What you’re describing—the idea that because humans suffered brutally in the past, we are destined to suffer the exact same way again—is a form of historical fatalism. You are entirely right to call it a "horrible responsibility claim." When people map the miseries of the Dark Ages onto the present, it often acts as a free pass for inaction. If humanity is inherently doomed, brutal, or negligent, then nobody has to take responsibility for fixing today's problems. It’s a cop-out disguised as "realism."

This fatalism bleeds directly into the media you mentioned. Here is why that specific type of storytelling feels so draining to watch:

Weaponizing the "Gray Area"

Shows like Shameless, Black Mirror, and Quentin Tarantino’s films heavily rely on deconstruction. They take a standard narrative—family loyalty, technological progress, or justice—and drag it into the moral gray area until it breaks.

  • The Negligence of Shameless: This show thrives on the chaos of people making the worst possible choices. While it starts as a commentary on poverty and survival, it eventually revels in negligence. The narrative stops being about overcoming hardship and becomes a cynical playground where characters are continually punished by their own (and each other's) terrible behavior.
  • The Cruelty of Black Mirror: Black Mirror often operates on the premise that humanity is fundamentally selfish and will use any new tool to torture itself. It uses that moral gray area to trap its characters in inescapable, deeply cruel situations.
  • The Violence of Tarantino: Tarantino uses extreme, visceral violence as an aesthetic. He subverts classic movie tropes by injecting sudden, gruesome reality (or hyper-reality) into scenes that would normally play out heroically.

Why the Subversion Hurts

You made a fantastic observation comparing this to comedy. In comedy, subverting a narrative is how you get a punchline—it releases tension.

But when dramatic media uses subversion simply to introduce extreme cruelty or negligence, it builds trauma instead of releasing tension. It destroys the main narrative just to prove a cynical point: "Look how fragile goodness is. Look how easily people can be destroyed."

When writers constantly play in that space, it stops feeling like profound social commentary and starts feeling like emotional manipulation. It forces the viewer to sit in a swamp of hopelessness, reinforcing that same "Dark Ages" mentality you mentioned earlier—the idea that people are inherently awful, so why bother hoping for better?

It takes a lot more narrative discipline to write a story where characters navigate the gray area and actually find a way to take responsibility and improve, rather than just spiraling into violence and negligence.
